Permissions, locks and unlocks

What can change, and which tokens become available next?

Creator powers: mint, freeze, fees & transfers

What can change after you buy?

Supply and powers are separate checks

Check tokens already held and permissions that can change supply or trading. A small creator balance can still matter if an authority allows more issuance or transfer restrictions.

For standard Solana tokens, start with mint and freeze authorities. For Token-2022 and other chains, inspect applicable extensions, contract roles, upgrades, and administrators.

PowerWhat could happenEvidence to save
Mint more unitsMore tokens become availableAuthority, enforced cap, issuance transactions
Freeze accountsAffected accounts cannot transfer while frozenFreeze authority and account status
Restrict transfersSome users or routes may be blockedRules, controller, exemptions
Change feesSelling costs or net receipts changeRate, cap, controller, activation rules
Upgrade logicPreviously checked behavior changesAdministrator and governance conditions

How many more can they mint?

If minting is enabled, find the enforced cap and who can use the authority. If no cap can be verified, future issuance remains unresolved. If the authority is permanently revoked under the relevant standard mechanism, record that minting path as disabled and continue checking other controls.

How to investigate it

  1. Open the mint/contract and check its owner program.
  2. Open authority details. Read mint, freeze, and metadata/update labels separately. A generic Authority summary may show only one type.
  3. Save each authority address or revoked status, source, and time. Use decoded mint data or a supported contract inspector for fields the summary does not expose.
  4. Check relevant extensions, roles, fee settings, caps, and delays.
  5. Open ordinary-wallet sales and failed transaction reasons. Record the applicable settings. A quote or simulation may change before execution.

Practical case — illustrative

At 09:20 UTC, SAMPLE uses a standard token program. Its mint and freeze authorities have been revoked, and this example has no additional transfer controls. Record those sources. The group still holds 12m available units, exceeding our example concentration limit.

Keep this record

Save an authority table: control, controller/status, possible action, source, time, unresolved question. Use entries such as “mint authority revoked” or “fee-change controller not found.”

Add these findings to your review worksheet →

Check your understanding — answered

Minting is disabled. What remains to check? Existing holdings, other powers, unlocks, liquidity, and buyers.

One address sold. Is that enough? Check exemptions and recent ordinary-wallet sales under the current settings.

The explorer does not show a freeze field. What should I write? Mark it unverified and identify the decoded data or program rules needed.

Float, locks, vesting & unlocks

Which inventory can reach the market now—or later?

Total supply is not sellable supply

Providers define total supply, circulating supply, and float differently. Record the definition beside the number. Separate pool reserves, burned units, locked allocations, treasury units, and ordinary balances.

For our example screen, use Section 5's available holder units. If restrictions or custody are unclear, record known quantities and leave the float-based percentage unresolved. Transferable units can also be difficult to sell if liquidity is thin.

What does locked mean?

A token lock or vesting contract controls when specified units become available. A cliff releases an amount on a date. Periodic vesting releases amounts on a schedule. Units may already be claimable while the contract has months left.

A liquidity lock concerns a specified liquidity position. Check both records. Platform rules and project terms determine whether either lock is required.

How to investigate it

  1. Open the public lock/vesting link. Compare its token address and chain.
  2. Read contract details in the provider's dashboard. For Streamflow, use the vesting contract details and documented schedule. Research does not require claiming tokens or signing a transaction.
  3. Record deposited, withdrawn, unlocked but unclaimed, and still-locked amounts. Check definitions to avoid double counting.
  4. Record start, cliff, amount per release, next release, and end with timezone.
  5. Check beneficiary, cancellation, and recipient-change rights. Streamflow cancellation, when permitted, can return unvested units to the sender. Include that possibility in your record.
FieldSAMPLE at 09:25 UTC on Day 1What to record
Team vesting allocation20mAdditional to the group's 12m available units
Already claimable0None available from this contract now
Next release4m at 09:00 UTC on Day 2Available holder supply can rise to 104m
Locked after release16mFuture releases to track
CancellationDisabled in this exampleVerify the actual rights for a real contract

Practical case — illustrative

After tomorrow's 4m unlock, group available holdings would be 16m and available holder supply 104m, assuming no other changes. 16m ÷ 104m = about 15.4%. Refresh the calculation after actual transactions.

The release makes tokens available. Watch subsequent transactions to learn whether the team sells them.

Keep this record

Save an unlock calendar: contract, beneficiary, next release time/timezone, units, claimable amount, controller rights, and source. Separate today's holdings from possible holdings after release.

Add these findings to your review worksheet →

Check your understanding — answered

The lock ends in a year. Can anything be sold today? Check already claimable units and holdings outside the lock.

Unlock tomorrow: will the team sell? Record the amount and watch transactions after release.

Should treasury units be excluded from float? Verify restrictions first; the treasury label does not establish a lock.
